message:
SITUATION:
Our engineering department went fully remote at the start of the year. In the following quarter, tickets closed per engineer fell 10% compared with the quarter before. Our VP says this proves remote work lowered productivity and wants people back in the office. In the same quarter, though, we hired four new engineers who were still onboarding, and the team switched to writing bigger tickets that bundle several tasks. I think the VP is wrong, and it's obviously just the new hires dragging the average down. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
Going remote lowered the engineering team's productivity.

RESPONSE:
I can't settle it with this data, and neither of you has proven your case. The VP's conclusion doesn't hold, but "obviously just the new hires" overreaches too.

## Why the VP's claim doesn't follow

Three things changed in the same quarter: remote work, four onboarding engineers, and bigger tickets. A 10% drop in tickets per engineer can't be pinned on one of them. Two problems stand out:

- **The ticket change breaks the metric.** If tickets now bundle several tasks, fewer tickets can mean the same or *more* work. Tickets closed before and after the change aren't comparable units. This alone could produce a 10% drop, or hide a gain.
- **One quarter is one data point.** Without the usual quarter-to-quarter variation, you don't know if 10% is unusual. Seasonality (holidays, planning cycles, a big release) could matter as well.

## Why your claim is also too strong

- **It depends on team size.** If four new hires produce about half a normal engineer's output, the drag on the average is roughly (4 / team size) × 50%. That's about 10% for a 20-person team, about 5% for a team of 40, and about 2.5% for a team of 80. On a larger team, new hires alone probably can't account for 10%.
- **The ticket-size change is at least as likely an explanation**, and you dropped it from your own argument.
- **Remote work could still have some effect.** It might be negative, neutral, or positive. Its effect could also be mixed into the onboarding: remote onboarding is sometimes slower, which would make your explanation partly the VP's.

## How to actually test it

1. **Exclude the new hires.** Compare tickets per engineer for engineers who were there in both quarters. If the drop disappears, your explanation gains a lot of support. If it remains, it doesn't.
2. **Normalize for ticket size.** Use story points, subtasks, linked PRs, or merged commits/PRs per engineer, whatever existed consistently in both periods. Better still, re-count the new quarter's tickets as their component tasks.
3. **Get a baseline.** Pull 4 to 8 prior quarters to see normal variation and seasonal patterns.
4. **Look at other signals.** Cycle time, deploy frequency, incident or bug rates, and whether roadmap commitments were met. Ticket counts are a weak productivity measure even without these confounds.
5. **Look forward.** Next quarter the new hires will be more ramped up and the ticket format will be stable. That gives a cleaner comparison against itself, though it still won't have an in-office control group.

Even after all this, you'd have a before/after comparison with no control group. That can weaken or support a causal story but can't prove it. What you *can* say firmly now is that a 10% drop in tickets closed, in a quarter when ticket definitions changed and the team grew, doesn't show that remote work lowered productivity. It also doesn't show that new hires caused the drop.

If you can export the ticket data (assignee, close date, start dates, any size estimates), I can run steps 1 to 3 for you.
